r: IND 1000 orients students to industrial design careers, employment trends, academic pathways, and a first pass at the design process, in a one-credit survey format built around discussion and information synthesis. Compiling career-option overviews, industry-trend summaries, and professional-requirement checklists maps closely to Getting Information and Updating and Using Relevant Knowledge, tasks observed-usage data already shows AI handling competently in office and advisory contexts. Because the deliverables are informational rather than physical, verification burden and embodiment offer little protection here. What holds the rating at Medium rather than higher is structural: the course is the explicit prerequisite for Design Aesthetics and Digital Composition, making it foundational scaffolding the program depends on. At 24 months, AI can already draft career overviews competently, but the course's gatekeeping role for the sequence keeps the instrumental need from collapsing to Low.

By 2031, AI assistants will fluently generate detailed industrial-design career guides, trend analyses, and employment-requirement summaries, and task-exposure research consistently classifies this kind of informational synthesis among the more automatable knowledge-work categories. The instrumental case for a live orientation course to deliver this content further erodes; a prospective student could plausibly assemble an equivalent picture of the field independently. What prevents the rating from rising past Medium is the course's foundational scaffolding role: it remains the formal prerequisite gating entry into Design Aesthetics and Digital Composition, and that structural dependency does not loosen on a five-year catalog-revision horizon. No accreditation or licensure mandate is in play. The rating holds Medium, with the caveat that the orientation content itself is now almost entirely reproducible by AI, leaving the prerequisite-gate function as the sole binding constraint.

A decade out, the central case has AI serving as a capable, personalized career and curriculum advisor for prospective design students, fully able to reproduce the informational content this course currently delivers about the field, employment trends, and academic requirements. Under a wide-uncertainty framing, it is plausible that such advising becomes largely self-service well before 2036. Yet the course's structural function as gateway to Design Aesthetics and Digital Composition is an institutional fact about MSU Denver's curriculum sequencing, not a capability question, and nothing in the evidence base suggests programs abandon prerequisite structures merely because content generation becomes cheap. The rating holds Medium, anchored entirely by foundational scaffolding rather than by any residual task difficulty; the honest uncertainty concerns whether the course is restructured around AI advising tools, not whether some gateway requirement persists.
IND 1000.d: This course defines, describes, and explains opportunities in the field of industrial design. It identifies and allows for the discussion of career options, evaluates employment trends in the field, and reviews academic and professional requirements for entry into the field. Instruction and background in the use of the design process for industrial design is also provided.

r: The applied work in IND 1010 is physical: selecting wood species, running a fabrication plan through wood-working tools and machines, constructing a furniture piece, and applying finishing materials. These tasks map to Handling and Moving Objects and Controlling Machines and Processes, categories task-exposure research places firmly outside AI's current reach, since no model operates a table saw or sands a joint. AI can help draft a design brief or generate furniture concepts, but the course's instrumental purpose is the student's own acquisition of shop competence and material judgment through hands-on construction. No accreditation mandate is named, so embodiment alone does the protective work. At 24 months, AI assists the conceptual front end of the design process while leaving the fabrication core, which is what the course is graded on, entirely untouched.

By 2031, generative design tools will more fluently propose furniture forms and cutting plans, and CNC-linked software will handle more of the layout work, shifting some conceptual labor off the student. But the graded competence in this course is physical fabrication skill itself — tool handling, machine operation, and finishing technique — which remains embodied and psychomotor, a category task-exposure research does not classify as automatable. Verification of safe, competent shop practice still requires a present, trained human who can catch an unsafe setup before it causes injury. No licensure or accreditation lock applies; embodiment is the entire constraint. The instrumental case for physically building the piece stays intact across a catalog-revision horizon, even as AI increasingly assists the design ideation that precedes construction. The rating remains Low, unchanged from the 24-month assessment.

Over a decade, additive manufacturing and robotic fabrication could plausibly absorb more routine wood-shop production in industrial settings, and the base automatability of some cutting and joinery tasks ticks upward under an aggressive capability scenario. Even so, the pedagogical purpose of IND 1010 — a student personally developing safe, competent hand-and-machine technique and material judgment — is not delivered by an AI system on the learner's behalf, and that embodied skill-acquisition function does not disappear even where industrial production automates further. The wide-uncertainty caveat applies more to how much of the fabrication economy shifts to automated production than to whether a design student still needs to learn wood-working technique directly. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment rather than by any expectation that the underlying tasks stay unautomated industry-wide.
IND 1010.d: An introductory course designed to give the student basic information about wood material properties, species selection criteria, practical design applications, and ordering and specifying protocol. The design process is presented and applied in the development of a furniture design and a fabrication plan, which is utilized to construct the design. The course also provides instruction for basic skill development in the use of wood working tools, machines, and processes. Wood finishing materials and processes are also studied and utilized in student projects.

r: IND 1100 teaches safe, competent use of tools across the woods, metals, and plastics labs: material-property fundamentals, fabrication and finishing technique, and shop safety and emergency procedure. The graded work is manual execution under real hazard conditions — operating shared equipment, following safety protocol, completing simple multi-material design projects — which maps to Handling and Moving Objects and Controlling Machines and Processes, categories task-exposure research places among the least automatable. Verification burden is meaningfully elevated because a lapse in shop-safety judgment carries real injury risk, so a present, trained human is required, not merely a knowledgeable one. The course is also the formal prerequisite for Materials II, giving it foundational scaffolding weight within the program. At 24 months, none of AI's growing content-generation capability touches the embodied core the course exists to teach.

By 2031, AI will more capably generate project concepts and specification sheets for multi-material fabrication, but the instrumental purpose of IND 1100 is not conceptual output — it is developing the physical competence and safety judgment to operate wood, metal, and plastics equipment without incident. That is exactly the high-verification-burden, embodied work that task-exposure research and the jagged-frontier evidence both flag as resistant: an AI recommendation about tool use carries no accountability if a student is injured following it. The course's role as prerequisite for Materials II further caps any erosion, since the program's fabrication sequence depends on this foundation being met in person. No accreditation lock exists, but embodiment and verification burden jointly hold the rating at Low across a catalog-revision horizon.

A decade of capability growth may make AI genuinely useful for pre-lab safety briefings, project planning, and material selection guidance, and adjacent industrial fabrication will likely see more automation. But the specific instrumental need IND 1100 satisfies — a student's own supervised, hands-on acquisition of tool competence and hazard judgment across three material shops — is not something an AI system performs for the learner, and the prerequisite relationship to Materials II keeps the course structurally load-bearing regardless of how automatable adjacent design tasks become. The central case through 2036 still has design students physically training in shop safety before advancing; the genuine uncertainty is about how much simulation or VR pre-training supplements the hands-on requirement, not about whether the embodied requirement itself is eliminated. Rating holds Low.
IND 1100.d: This course is an introduction to working safely and efficiently with tools in the woods, metals, and plastics labs. Students will study basic information about material properties and learn fundamental fabrication and finishing techniques through various simple design projects incorporating wood, metal, and plastic materials. Lectures will also cover shop tools and considerations, along with safety and emergency procedures.

r: IND 1130 introduces forming, casting, and reinforced-plastic manufacturing processes through direct examination and, implicitly, hands-on process work typical of the department's materials-and-fabrication sequence. These processes map to Controlling Machines and Processes and Monitoring Processes, Materials, or Surroundings — physical, equipment-mediated tasks that task-exposure research consistently places outside AI's current competence. AI can summarize plastics-forming theory or compare process trade-offs in text, but it cannot heat, mold, or cure a part, and the course's instrumental purpose is developing the student's physical process literacy. No accreditation or licensure mandate is described. At 24 months the rating is Low, driven entirely by the embodied, equipment-dependent nature of learning manufacturing processes rather than by any institutional lock. The description here is comparatively general, which tempers confidence.

By 2031, AI process-simulation tools will likely model plastics-forming outcomes more accurately, offloading some pre-production analysis and troubleshooting from students. But the course's applied competence remains physically executing forming, casting, and reinforcement techniques, and evaluating whether a molded or cast part meets specification still benefits from hands-on familiarity with material behavior under heat and pressure — a verification task tied to physical judgment rather than pure computation. No accreditation lock applies, so embodiment alone protects the rating. Across a catalog-revision horizon, the instrumental need to physically practice these manufacturing processes is not meaningfully eroded by better simulation software, even as such tools increasingly assist the conceptual planning that surrounds hands-on fabrication. Rating remains Low, with confidence tempered by the description's generality.

Ten years out, industrial plastics manufacturing will likely be more automated end-to-end, and simulation-driven process design could be commonplace, nudging the underlying task-automatability upward under an aggressive scenario. Still, the pedagogical function of IND 1130 — a student personally examining and executing forming, casting, and reinforcement processes to build physical-material intuition — is not substituted by industry automation trends, since the course exists to train the person, not to produce the part. The uncertainty here is genuinely wide: how much of plastics fabrication instruction shifts toward simulation versus retained hands-on practice is an open pedagogical question this brief general description cannot resolve with confidence. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment, with lower confidence reflecting the course's thin catalog description relative to its peers.
IND 1130.d: This course is an introduction to the basic manufacturing processes and techniques used in the plastics industries. A variety of forming, casting, and reinforced plastic processes will be examined.

r: IND 1250 covers sheet-metal manipulation, machining, welding, fastening, and bench metalworking, plus mechanical, sandblasting, polishing, and painting finishing techniques, applied through short-term design projects. This is hazardous, tool- and machine-mediated physical work — welding and machining in particular carry real injury risk — mapping to Controlling Machines and Processes and Handling and Moving Objects, categories task-exposure research treats as low-exposure. Verification burden is elevated: a welded joint or machined tolerance must be checked by someone who understands metal behavior, not merely described accurately in text. AI can help draft a metalworking design brief, but cannot weld a seam or verify its structural soundness. No accreditation mandate is named. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on metalworking competence, including safety practice around welding and machining, is fully intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted design tools will more capably generate metal-fabrication concepts and cutting layouts, but the graded core of IND 1250 is physical execution — welding, machining, and finishing metal components safely and to specification. Verification of weld integrity, machined tolerances, and finish quality depends on trained physical judgment and instrumentation the student learns to use in person, not on text-based AI output; the jagged-frontier problem is acute where a plausible-looking but structurally unsound weld carries real safety consequences. No accreditation lock protects the course, but the embodied, high-verification-burden nature of metalworking does. Across a catalog-revision horizon, the rating stays Low: better AI design assistance changes the ideation phase surrounding the project, not the requirement that a student personally practice metal fabrication and safety discipline.

A decade out, robotic welding and CNC metal machining will be more pervasive in industry, and it is plausible that some routine production metalwork automates substantially by 2036. But IND 1250 exists to train the student's own competence — bench metalworking skill, welding technique, safety judgment around hazardous processes — and that pedagogical function does not disappear because industrial production automates around it, any more than automated manufacturing eliminates the need for engineers to understand fabrication. The genuine uncertainty is how much simulation or robotic-assisted training supplements hands-on instruction by 2036, not whether the embodied skill requirement itself is removed. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by the elevated verification burden inherent to welding and machining safety, which no text-based system can discharge on the student's behalf.
IND 1250.d: This course covers the manipulation of sheet metal, machining of metals, welding of metals, fasteners, and bench metal working. Finishing of metals is also covered, including mechanical processes, sandblasting, polishing, and painting techniques. Emphasis is placed on factors necessary to create products that involve metals and metal components. The design process is introduced and applied in the development of short-term design projects.

r: IND 1300 has students apply advanced woods, metals, and plastics fabrication techniques to manufacture an original product against an assigned design brief, then document the process in construction drawings and presentation materials. The manufacturing core — material selection, machine operation, physical construction — maps to Controlling Machines and Processes and Handling and Moving Objects, low-exposure categories in task-exposure research, while the documentation layer maps to Drafting and Documenting/Recording Information and is more AI-assisted. Because the course's binding grade centers on physically manufacturing the product, not merely documenting it, embodiment is the constraint that governs the rating. IND 1100 is a listed prerequisite, giving the course moderate foundational weight within the sequence. At 24 months, AI can help generate presentation graphics, but the fabrication requirement at the course's core is untouched.

By 2031, AI design and documentation tools will more fluently generate construction drawings and polished presentation materials, further automating the paperwork layer of the course. That narrows what remains distinctively human, but the graded core — manufacturing an original design through advanced wood, metal, and plastics fabrication technique — stays embodied and resistant to substitution, since no AI system can build the physical object on the student's behalf. Verification that a fabricated product actually meets the design brief's material and construction requirements still depends on physically inspecting the piece. No accreditation lock applies. Across a catalog-revision horizon the instrumental need to physically manufacture the product is preserved even as the surrounding documentation tasks become nearly fully AI-assisted, holding the rating at Low.

A decade out, generative design and AI-assisted drafting will likely handle construction-drawing and presentation-material production almost entirely, and base task-automatability for the course as a whole ticks upward accordingly. But the central deliverable — a student personally fabricating an original product using advanced multi-material technique — remains an embodied act that AI does not perform for the learner, even under an aggressive capability scenario for adjacent design documentation. The honest uncertainty concerns how much of the course's grading weight could shift toward AI-assisted documentation and away from hands-on construction, a pedagogical choice rather than a capability constraint. As currently structured around physical fabrication, the rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment rather than by any expectation that the documentation tasks stay unautomated.
IND 1300.d: This studio and lecture course helps students apply advanced woods, metals, and plastics fabrication techniques to create original products. Students design and manufacture items in response to an assigned design brief through appropriate design considerations and material selection. The design process is documented throughout the semester to generate a detailed set of construction drawings and presentation materials.

r: IND 1450 teaches production-drawing creation using manual drafting tools and CAD software, hand lettering, orthographic projection, GD&T, and generating CNC data for part production. This is predominantly digital, computer-mediated work — Interacting With Computers and Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices, Parts, and Equipment — a category observed-usage data shows is already heavily used, and generative CAD tools can already produce competent orthographic and dimensioned drawings from a design brief. The verification requirement is moderate: GD&T errors and CNC data mistakes propagate into fabricated parts, so a knowledgeable human still checks output. No licensure or accreditation mandate is described, and the course is only moderately foundational within the batch. At 24 months, AI already performs meaningful portions of routine technical drawing, though full CAD-to-CNC production drawings still need expert review, keeping the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, generative CAD and AI drafting assistants will plausibly produce complete, standards-compliant production drawings and CNC toolpaths from a specification with limited human intervention, consistent with GDPval evidence that AI models are approaching parity on real occupational deliverables in digital domains. The instrumental case for a student manually producing every orthographic view and GD&T callout weakens substantially. No accreditation lock or deep foundational role protects the course from this erosion — it is a digital-production skill course without institutional insulation. The rating rises to High: the applied tasks the course teaches are squarely inside AI's growing competence, and diffusion of CAD-integrated AI tools into design workflows and firms is plausible well within five years, even if industry-wide adoption remains uneven at that point.

A decade out, the central case has AI-generated technical drawings and CNC data production as standard practice, with human designers directing specifications and validating outputs rather than manually drafting them. Task-exposure research's finding that programming- and specification-adjacent tasks are strongly positively associated with exposure applies directly to CAD production work. The course's instrumental rationale shifts from teaching manual drafting execution toward teaching the standards needed to specify and check AI-generated output — a real function, but one this course as currently described does not emphasize. With no accreditation lock or strong foundational role to cap the erosion, the rating holds High, with the caveat that how CAD instruction is restructured around AI tools by 2036 is genuinely uncertain, and that human specification-writing skill could yet resurface as a narrower verification role.
IND 1450.d: An introductory course designed to give students information about creating production drawings. The technical drawing process is presented and applied to a variety of products using both manual drafting tools and computer software. Additional topics include hand lettering, orthographic projections, Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD & T), and creating Computer Numerical Controlled (CNC) data for part production. The design process is addressed with the aid of a short-term design project with accompanying technical drawings and CNC production.

r: IND 1470 develops the specific psychomotor and perceptual skill of representing objects through hand-drawn perspective, shading, and graphic technique — training the eye and hand together to render visual reality on paper. Although generative image models can already produce polished renderings from a text prompt, that substitutes for the deliverable, not for the competence the course builds: the student's own capacity to observe, interpret, and render form by hand. This is embodied, psychomotor skill acquisition analogous to studio drawing and painting instruction, a category task-exposure research does not treat as automatable because the instrumental purpose is the human act itself, not merely the picture produced. No accreditation mandate is described. At 24 months the rating is Low, held by embodiment rather than by any institutional lock, even as AI image generation grows more capable in parallel.

By 2031, AI image generation will be markedly more capable and will reshape parts of the commercial illustration and rendering economy — a labor-market question explicitly outside this rating. Whether a design student still needs to develop hand-drawing technique is a separate question, and the answer is unchanged: the graphic-representation skill this course builds is a physical, perceptual-motor competence that AI performs on the student's behalf in name only, by producing a substitute image rather than teaching the underlying observational skill. There is no accreditation lock; embodiment alone protects the rating across a catalog-revision horizon. The instrumental case for hand-drawing instruction holds at Low, even as the broader market for hand-rendered deliverables in industry practice likely continues shrinking and firms lean harder on generated imagery for client-facing work.

Over a decade, generative image tools will be woven pervasively through visual-communication practice, and the wide-uncertainty caveat is real for how much hand-rendering survives as a professional deliverable in industrial design workflows by 2036. But Design Drawing Techniques builds an embodied human competence — perceptual accuracy and hand control in representing form — that is not a task AI executes for the learner, since the pedagogical act is the student's own skill development, not the image output. The most plausible ten-year shift is in how much hand-drawing instruction is retained relative to digital rendering in the broader curriculum, a pedagogical choice, not a capability constraint. The rating stays Low, anchored in embodiment even as the surrounding market for rendered images transforms.
IND 1470.d: This course introduces students to the basic concepts and skills used in industry to communicate ideas through a hand- drawn, two-dimensional format. Students will develop drawing skills which represent objects as the eye sees them using perspective, shading, and a variety of graphic techniques. Instruction and practice incorporates the study of visual reality, graphic form, visual impact, and the logic and proof of what we see.

r: IND 2000 develops visual literacy and form-development skill through both 2D and 3D approaches to the elements and principles of design, with an explicit emphasis on visualization technique. The work mixes conceptual composition judgment, which AI image and design tools already assist meaningfully, with physical form-development exercises that keep part of the course embodied — a mixed profile rather than a clean digital or physical category. Judging the Qualities of Objects and Thinking Creatively are the relevant activities, and evaluative design judgment is not yet reliably automated at production quality. IND 1000 is a listed prerequisite, giving the course moderate foundational weight for the design sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop the student's own visual-design judgment through mixed 2D/3D practice is not meaningfully eroded.

By 2031, AI design tools will more capably generate and critique compositions across 2D and 3D form studies, consistent with task-exposure evidence that visual and creative production tasks are increasingly within AI's competence even where critical judgment resists it. The instrumental case shifts: a student can generate more raw visual material faster, but the course's purpose — developing personal aesthetic judgment and visualization skill applicable across media — is not fully delivered by that generation. With no accreditation lock and only moderate foundational weight, the rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion in the mechanical production of visual studies while the underlying design-judgment competence, and its role feeding later coursework, keeps the course from falling to Low or rising to High.

A decade out, AI tools will plausibly generate sophisticated 2D and 3D form studies and offer detailed compositional critique, further narrowing the distinctively human production tasks in the course. But cultivating a student's own aesthetic judgment — the ability to evaluate and direct form development rather than merely generate it — remains a meaningful instrumental purpose, and mixed physical-digital form work retains some embodied component that resists full substitution, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that critical evaluative skill is negatively associated with exposure even as generative production skews positively. The uncertainty is genuinely wide regarding how much of design-principles instruction becomes AI-critique-driven by 2036, and whether physical maquette-building survives as a graded requirement. The rating holds Medium, reflecting substantial but incomplete erosion of the applied production tasks the course currently emphasizes, capped by the course's continuing role feeding later design coursework.
IND 2000.d: Students will investigate and practice the basic visual elements and principles of design through both 2D and 3D approaches. Emphasis will be placed on form development and visualization techniques.

r: IND 2100 trains students to capture original work digitally, edit it with computer software, and compose presentation-page layouts for department portfolio review, through studio and location photographic projects. The editing and layout work is Interacting With Computers and Documenting/Recording Information — categories observed-usage data already shows are among the heaviest AI use areas — and AI photo-editing and layout tools already perform competent composition work. The image-capture step retains a physical, location-based component, operating a camera on-site, which keeps part of the course embodied. Because portfolio-review preparation functions as an internal program gate, the course carries moderate foundational weight even without formal accreditation. At 24 months, AI meaningfully assists the editing and layout stages, but the photographic capture and the student's own compositional decision-making keep the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, AI editing and automated page-layout tools will plausibly handle the bulk of the software-based composition work this course teaches, and generative and computational photography tools will increasingly assist even the capture stage through automated framing and enhancement. Task-exposure research's finding that digital, computer-mediated tasks skew heavily toward automatability applies directly here. The course carries no accreditation lock, and its foundational role is limited to an internal portfolio-review gate rather than a hard prerequisite chain, so that scaffolding function does not restrain the rating on a five-year horizon. With the digital-composition tasks increasingly AI-executable and few protective factors remaining, the rating rises to High. The physical photography component provides only partial insulation, since the graded deliverable is the edited, composed presentation artifact, not the raw capture, and observed-usage patterns already show editing and layout work concentrated in AI's most-used categories.

A decade out, AI-driven photo editing, compositional layout, and even automated image capture and framing will plausibly be standard tools in design-portfolio production, consistent with the central case that digital creative-production tasks continue automating faster than embodied ones. The course's instrumental rationale for teaching manual software editing and layout technique is substantially eroded under this scenario, even though a student's compositional eye and curatorial judgment retain some residual value in directing AI tools toward a coherent portfolio. With no institutional lock to cap the erosion, the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty concerns how portfolio-review expectations themselves evolve once AI composition tools are ubiquitous, not whether the current digital-production tasks remain resistant to automation, and whether the location-photography step retains any distinct instructional weight.
IND 2100.d: This lecture/lab course prepares students to capture their original works digitally with various documenting equipment and to edit them with computer software. Studio and location photographic projects require students to use the camera for documentation, research and communication. Visual compositions that include digital and nondigital elements and presentation page layout principals will be introduced and practiced for students' department portfolio review preparation.

r: IND 2450 asks students to run the full design process in a studio setting: researching historical precedent and market trends, generating and refining concepts, and producing polished portfolio page layouts against departmental screening criteria. The documentation and research components — market-trend synthesis, page-layout production — sit inside task-exposure research's highly-exposed writing-and-office-tasks band, and observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and writing categories dominating current deployment. Aesthetic refinement and studio critique, though, depend on a developing personal design sensibility that a model does not build for the student. No licensure or accreditation mandate protects the course, but it functions as prerequisite substrate for the later studio sequence. At 24 months the instrumental case is only lightly eroded: AI can draft research summaries or clean up layouts, but the core studio judgment this early course cultivates is not yet substitutable.

By 2031, AI image and layout tools will competently produce concept sketches, market-research syntheses, and finished portfolio pages, and productivity research on professional writing and design-adjacent tasks points to sizable time savings for exactly this kind of documentation work. The instrumental case for having students perform the mechanical portfolio-production tasks weakens materially. What remains harder to substitute is the iterative aesthetic judgment developed through studio critique — evaluating, revising, and defending design choices — which the course still trains through direct instructor feedback. Because IND 2450 seeds skills the later required studio sequence builds on, foundational scaffolding caps how far the rating can rise even as the surrounding production tasks become AI-competent. The rating moves to Medium: execution increasingly automates, but the underlying design-judgment substrate the major depends on has not yet been supplanted.

A decade out, generative design and layout tools should handle most of the documentation and research-synthesis work this course currently assigns, and capability-trend evidence suggests the tasks AI handles keep expanding in scope over time. Even so, the course's foundational role — training the studio design process and critique habits later required courses assume students already have — keeps a floor under its instrumental necessity; wide uncertainty about adoption pace does not remove that scaffolding function. The most plausible shift is pedagogical: less time on manual layout production, more on directing and evaluating AI-generated design options and defending an aesthetic point of view. The rating holds Medium, anchored by foundational role rather than by any institutional mandate, which this course notably lacks.
IND 2450.d: In laboratory and studio environments, the design process is introduced and practiced as students apply learned fundamental skills, critical thinking, problem solving, and aesthetic refinement to assigned design projects. Students are required to address the historical context of their designs as they research technological evolution, market trends, aesthetic preferences, and consumer behavior. Students are required to document their work and create page layouts that depict and describe their projects according to the Department portfolio screening criteria.

r: This non-majors course has students apply fundamental design principles directly to physical three-dimensional forms: building sketches into drawings and hand-built models, then writing research reports and presenting the resulting concepts. The model-making and hands-on construction of study models sit squarely in the physical, psychomotor task categories that task-exposure research consistently classifies as low-exposure, even though the accompanying research reports are more automatable. There is no accreditation or licensure mandate protecting the course — it exists purely as a design-literacy elective for non-majors — and it is not prerequisite substrate for further required coursework. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically build and present a model is essentially unaffected: a model can help draft the report, but it does not construct the object the student is graded on making with their hands.

By 2031, AI drafting tools will handle the research-report and presentation-narrative components of this course fluently, echoing productivity research showing large gains on professional writing tasks. That leaves the physically embodied core — sketching by hand, constructing three-dimensional study models of forms and structures — essentially untouched, since manipulating materials and tools is not a task language or image models perform on the student's behalf. Diffusion data shows AI adoption still uneven across firms and contexts at this horizon, reinforcing that hands-on model-making pedagogy is unlikely to be displaced by tool availability. With no institutional mandate and no foundational role to argue upward, the protective effect here comes entirely from embodiment. The rating stays Low: the course's instrumental purpose is the physical act of making, which AI does not perform for the learner.

Even under a central case of much stronger AI-assisted design tools by 2036, IND 2455 was built for non-majors to gain literacy through hands-on making — sketching, drawing, and physically constructing three-dimensional models — and that embodied task is not one capability growth substitutes away from the student. Task-exposure research's core distinction between manual/physical work and automatable knowledge work still applies at this horizon; the course sits firmly on the protected side. The presentation and reporting components will likely lean further on AI assistance, but that shift does not touch the instrumental rationale for the studio itself. With no accreditation lock and no foundational load-bearing role, the rating is protected purely by the embodied nature of the task. The rating holds Low, with genuine but narrow uncertainty about how much documentation work students still do unaided.
IND 2455.d: This course is for non-majors. In laboratory and studio environments, the design process is introduced and practiced as students apply fundamental principles to three-dimensional forms, structures, and products. Students address the historical context of their designs as they practice critical thinking, research, problem solving and aesthetic refinement. Students create sketches, drawings, models, research reports and presentation of their design concepts.

r: This lecture-and-discussion course examines how technology and design have shaped, and been shaped by, global cultures — communications, product design, food production, transportation, sustainability, and ethics viewed comparatively across societies. The applied work is research, synthesis, and written or discussed argument about historical and cross-cultural patterns, tasks that observed-usage data places within the largest current AI-use categories and that task-exposure research classifies as writing-adjacent and comparatively exposed. What holds the rating down is not embodiment — there is none here — but the GT-SS3 Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity designation, a statutory transfer-core mandate that keeps the course structurally required regardless of how automatable its content generation becomes. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can summarize global design history, but the general-education requirement that a student take this course does not change with it.

By 2031, language models will fluently synthesize the comparative technology-and-culture material this course covers and can already draft essays engaging its themes, sharpening the tension around the writing and analysis components. Productivity research on professional writing tasks suggests students could produce comparable work with substantially less independent effort, which meaningfully erodes the content-generation rationale for the course. What remains fixed on this horizon is the GT-Pathways transfer-core designation, a statutory requirement that does not lapse on a normal catalog-revision cycle; that mandate caps the rating rather than any protective task property. The instrumental case shifts from producing the analysis to demonstrating and defending it, a real change in what the course teaches. The rating rises to Medium, driven by high content-exposure but held there by the general-education lock.

A decade out, AI will be a fluent, well-informed interlocutor on the global history of technology and design, capable of generating comparative analysis on demand — a scope expansion capability-trend evidence on lengthening task horizons would predict. The instrumental rationale for a student personally producing this analysis is substantially eroded by that point. The GT-Pathways designation is the binding constraint through the horizon: absent a statewide policy change, the transfer-core requirement persists regardless of how thoroughly AI can perform the underlying analytical tasks. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical — how a course like this is taught and assessed once AI is a routine research partner — not whether the general-education mandate holds. The rating stays Medium, capped by institutional lock-in rather than by any inherent resistance of the coursework to automation.
IND 2810.d: This course teaches students about the relationship between technology, design, and global cultures. Historical perspectives provide a foundation for discussion about how technology and design have affected, and continue to affect, the daily lives of people throughout the world. Emphasis is placed on relevant technologies developed in societies outside the U.S., and on the effects that those technologies have had on global societies, including the U.S. Particular attention is paid to communications, product design, food production, work and jobs, transportation, the military, sustainability, and ethical issues.

r: The course surveys mass-production manufacturing methods and materials so students can make appropriate material, process, and finishing selections for their own designed products — applied technical knowledge rather than hands-on fabrication.
